title: Redwood deep-dive: JSON mode / Tool-calling performance
next_steps: Sara to share JSON-mode benchmark spreadsheet and raw logs by 2025-05-23
Daniel to run a dedicated 1k-query KV-cache microbenchmark on Dedicated cluster and share results 2025-05-27
VertexEdge to provide representative prompt set and schema examples by 2025-05-22
Schedule on-prem pilot planning call (30m) w/ infra on 2025-05-29
action_items: Sara Kim - Share benchmark spreadsheet + runbook - 2025-05-23
Daniel Park - Run KV-cache + constrained decoding microbench on Dedicated (p50/p95/p99) - 2025-05-27
Priya Singh - Upload 50 sample prompt+schema pairs to shared drive - 2025-05-22

summary: Technical deep-dive focusing on JSON mode / function calling overhead, constrained decoding, and runtime optimizations (KV cache, batching, quantization). Customer is evaluating Dedicated and Private (VPC/on-prem) for latency-sensitive structured outputs. Next steps: share benchmarks, run microbenchmarks on Dedicated, and plan on-prem pilot.
transcript: [00:00] Sara Kim: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, we'll do a deep dive into our JSON / tool calling perf. daniel and i will share results and then go into kv cache and batching tradeoffs

[00:12] Michael Torres: thanks sara. bit of context: we're building an inference pipeline that needs structured JSON outputs for downstream ingestion. latency requirement is tight - 90th perc under 350ms for short prompts (~200 tokens) - and cost matters.
[00:30] Daniel Park: got it. quick qual - are you leaning hosted, Dedicated, or private? or evaluating all three?

[00:36] Priya Singh: we're primarily looking at Dedicated for predictable throughput, but we need a Private / on-prem option for a subset of regulated customers. also curious about how function-calling / json mode affects latency and token cost.
[00:50] Hannah Lee: security is a blocker for some clients - SSO / SAML and KMS integration must be available for Private. also audit logs and retention settings.

[01:02] Sara Kim: yes we support SAML, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs; we'll attach our security pack. today focus on performance: how constrained decoding / JSON mode increases generation overhead and what mitigations are available.

[01:20] Daniel Park: high-level: JSON mode (or function-calling) constrains the decoder which can add overhead because of token-level validation + constrained beam search or sampling restrictions. overhead depends on model, sequence length, and whether we're running quantized kernels or not.

[01:40] Daniel Park: for example, on a 16GB A100 Dedicated worker we saw an extra ~10-20% p50 latency when running strict JSON constraints versus freeform sampling for 150 token outputs - p95 can be higher depending on validation frequency.
[01:58] Priya Singh: is that because of repeated post-hoc validation loops? can you clarify the pipeline?

[02:05] Daniel Park: yeah so we do token-level constrained decoding with an accept/reject or mask application. On our runtime we try to push masks into the kernel when possible to avoid token-by-token CPU roundtrips, but some schemas require dynamic checks (e.g., nested object validation) which incurs extra kernels or CPU verification steps.
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: when you say mask pushed into kernel - does that work with quantized int8 kernels too? we're planning to use quantization to reduce cost.

[02:42] Daniel Park: good question. we have quantized execution paths where masks are supported, but the shape of the mask and the bitwidth can affect throughput. int8 kernels are faster per token but mask-application logic can reduce the speedup. practically we see ~1.6-1.9x speedup with q8 on unconstrained decoding; with heavy constraints it's closer to ~1.3-1.5x.

[03:05] Sara Kim: also worth calling out KV cache behavior: JSON mode often produces short, repetitive tokens for structural punctuation which can be cached. our prefix/KV cache reduces repeated attention computation across similar prompts or multi-turn flows.

[03:20] Michael Torres: can you run through a concrete benchmark - say 200 token prompt, targeting a 60-200 token completion producing JSON about 12 fields - what do you expect p95 latency on Dedicated?

[03:32] Daniel Park: on Dedicated A100 80GB reserved pool with our optimized kernels: unconstrained freeform completion p95 ~210ms for that shape; with strict JSON-mode constrained decoding p95 moved to ~290-320ms depending on schema complexity and validation frequency. with int8 quantization p95 unconstrained ~130-160ms but with constraints ~220-260ms.
[03:58] Priya Singh: that's helpful. what about throughput (rps) and batching? do you batch JSON-mode requests?

[04:06] Daniel Park: batching helps a lot for throughput but hurts tail latency. we use dynamic continuous batching in the runtime; for latency SLO we recommend small batch sizes or latency-prioritized lanes. If your requirement is p95 <350ms, we can configure dedicated pool with low-latency lane: small max-batch of 4 and pre-warm KV cache.
[04:30] Liam O'Connor: pre-warm how? like send synthetic prefixes?

[04:33] Daniel Park: two ways: 1) warm the KV cache with representative prompts during off-peak, stored per-model-prefix; 2) keep resident warm workers pinned with your model versions. both reduce cold-start and p95 effects.
[04:50] Michael Torres: are there specific schema patterns that exacerbate constrained decoding overhead?

[04:55] Daniel Park: yes - deeply nested JSON with validation on numeric ranges, or schema with lots of alternations (big choice sets) can blow up the mask complexity. Also when the model needs to call external tools mid-generation (tool-calling), we introduce small network/IO latencies for the tool invocation which add up if frequent.
[05:12] Priya Singh: tool-calling: we plan to use a local helper service that the model calls to validate or fetch ids. does that mean each tool call adds a round-trip? can Redwood pipeline those?

[05:21] Sara Kim: tool calls are basically synchronous RPCs in the default flow - yes each tool call introduces round-trip latency. we support async tool results with streaming or callbacks so you can pipeline some operations, but that requires a bit more orchestration on the client.

[05:40] Daniel Park: one pattern we recommend: push as much static validation offline (client-side) and reduce token-level validation during generation. Another is to use a constrained grammar that's simple enough to fit into kernel masks. For tool-calls do batching at the application layer: group validation calls to reduce per-call overhead.
[06:00] Michael Torres: ok, can you talk about the cost tradeoffs - if we go Dedicated + int8 quantization + small batch lanes, what's the delta vs hosted?

[06:10] Sara Kim: short answer: Dedicated with quantization gives better unit cost if you have sustained volume - but it requires reservation. Hosted simple pay-as-you-go is higher per-token but less operational overhead. We'll share cost models in the spreadsheet.

[06:25] Hannah Lee: for Private/on-prem, network topology is critical. if model-serving nodes call internal tools, we need to know egress constraints and whether the Redwood control plane communicates metadata. can you run through what contacts the control plane has?

[06:38] Daniel Park: for Private we can operate in air-gapped mode with local control plane and optional telemetry forwarding. If you require zero egress we can onboard an on-prem package; otherwise VPC-hosted Private clusters can NAT to our control plane endpoints for metrics and rollouts. we'll capture specifics in the security pack.
[06:58] Priya Singh: what metrics should we collect during the pilot to evaluate JSON-mode overhead?

[07:03] Daniel Park: collect token-level latencies, p50/p95/p99 for both total request and decode-only, number of tool-calls per request, cache hit ratio for KV cache, batch sizes, and CPU/GPU utilization. Also collect rejected token counts if you're applying strict schema masks.
[07:20] Michael Torres: do you have a simple microbenchmark we can run?

[07:24] Daniel Park: yes - we'll send a bench harness: 1) 1k warm requests with representative prompt+schema, 2) run with unconstrained, constrained JSON masks applied, and constrained + int8 quant. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[07:38] Sara Kim: note - sometimes the transcriptions of the mask application differs across model families; that affects results. we'll specify model family and kernel flags used for each run.
[07:50] Liam O'Connor: curious about KV cache scope - is it per model version, per client, per prompt prefix?

[07:56] Daniel Park: primary keys are model version + prefix hash + tenant id. you can configure either global-ish caches or tenant-specific caches. for multi-tenant Dedicated we do tenant partitioning to avoid leakage.
[08:10] Priya Singh: and cache eviction? LRU? TTL?

[08:13] Daniel Park: default is LRU with configurable TTL per workload. for structured output where prefixes are highly similar we recommend longer TTL and sticky workers to keep lower re-computation.
[08:26] Michael Torres: earlier you said token-level validation can be pushed into kernels - any limitations with Open-source models like LLaMA or Mistral variants?

[08:35] Daniel Park: kernel support depends on attention implementation and compiled operators. some OSS models have proprietary tokenizers or nonstandard EOS behavior which complicates masking; we generally test per-model. we'll include family-specific notes in the bench doc.
[08:50] Priya Singh: what about constrained decoding via constrained sampling (top-k/top-p adjustments) vs hard masks? Which is better for JSON correctness vs latency?

[08:58] Daniel Park: soft constraints (top-k/p tuning) are cheaper but less deterministic for strict JSON. Hard masks give determinism but higher compute overhead. Tradeoff: for 99% correctness you might use soft constraints + an offline validator, for 100% schema compliance use hard masks.

[09:18] Sara Kim: practical recommendation - start with soft constraints + post-validate in app layer; if you need strict, only move to hard masks for the subset of endpoints that require it. that combination usually hits latency/cost targets.
[09:31] Michael Torres: about tool-calling again - if a tool call fails mid-generation, what's Redwood's behavior? retry? fallbacks?

[09:38] Daniel Park: runtime supports graceful fallback policies - you can configure automatic fallback to a simpler schema or to a default object if tool fails, or bubble the error to the app. retries can be configured but add latency.
[09:50] Priya Singh: in the microbench, can you include scenarios with 0/1/2 tool-calls per request?
[09:55] Daniel Park: yes we'll include tool-call scenarios and synthetic latencies (50/100/200ms) to show sensitivity.
[10:05] Hannah Lee: security question - does constrained decoding or tool-calling expose more PII in logs?

[10:12] Sara Kim: logs and traces can be redacted per customer policy. audit logs record metadata and request hashes; you can opt into token-level logging but most customers redact tokens and only keep metadata and schema outcomes.
[10:25] Michael Torres: excellent. ok let's talk numbers again - Daniel, you mentioned p95 with quantized constraints ~220-260ms; what about p99?

[10:33] Daniel Park: p99 depends heavily on batching and network variability; typical p99 for constrained+quant on a Dedicated pool is ~380-480ms, but with a low-latency dedicated lane and warm caches we can push it under 350ms. that's why we've suggested lane-level config.
[10:55] Priya Singh: what's involved to set up a low-latency lane?
[10:59] Daniel Park: it's a Dedicated pool config: smaller max-batch, worker pinning, pre-warmed kernels, and higher cost for reserved capacity. we'll show the recommended configs in the spreadsheet.
[11:10] Michael Torres: network egress - in Private on-prem mode does the runtime still reach out for kernel updates or anything? we want to avoid surprises.
[11:18] Daniel Park: we can disable auto-updates; kernel patches are optional and can be applied manually. telemetry can be toggled. for air-gapped installs we provide offline packages.

[11:28] Sara Kim: short recap and concrete asks - VertexEdge to send prompt+schema samples and network topology; Redwood to run bench and share spreadsheet and security pack; schedule on-prem pilot planning. Agreed?
[11:40] Michael Torres: yes agreed. one more: can you include sample TFLOPS/GPU utilization graphs in the bench?
[11:46] Daniel Park: yep we'll include GPU util, mem pressure, and per-kernel breakdowns.
[11:52] Priya Singh: for the bench harness, what SDKs do you recommend? we use Python and a Go microservice for production glue.
[11:58] Sara Kim: Python SDK and a small Go client we provide for tool-calls. we'll attach quickstart snippets.
[12:05] Liam O'Connor: last ops Q - how do rolling model updates affect KV cache warming and tail latency?
[12:12] Daniel Park: rolling updates invalidate caches unless you pin model version. we recommend blue/green with pinned caches during rollout. KV cache warm-up should be part of the rollout plan.
[12:25] Michael Torres: great. thanks all. any other blockers?
[12:29] Hannah Lee: just security attachments - SAML metadata and KMS docs please.
[12:33] Sara Kim: will send.
[12:36] Daniel Park: i'll follow up with the bench harness and initial numbers. expect raw logs + a summarized spreadsheet.
[12:42] Michael Torres: thanks, talk soon.
[12:45] End of recording
